draft.title: Defences to negligence
card: A defence is an argument by the defendant that they should not have to pay the full amount, or anything at all, even if the plaintiff proves negligence.
the plaintiff did not take reasonable care for their own safety, and this helped cause their own harm. The court can reduce the damages to reflect the plaintiff's share of the blame.
the plaintiff knew about a specific risk and freely chose to accept it. If the defendant proves this, the claim can fail completely.
The difference is the result. Contributory negligence lowers the damages. Voluntary assumption of risk can defeat the claim.
draft.remember: Contributory negligence cuts the damages. Voluntary assumption of risk can defeat the claim.

a.q: A court finds a driver negligent, but the injured passenger was not wearing a seatbelt, which made their injuries worse. What is the likely effect of this defence?
opts: The damages are reduced to reflect the passenger's share
The claim fails completely and no damages are paid
The driver is found to owe no duty of care to the passenger
The damages are increased because the injuries were worse
a.why: Not wearing a seatbelt is a failure to take reasonable care for one's own safety, so it is contributory negligence. This reduces the damages. It does not defeat the claim, because the driver was still negligent.
a.clue: The passenger helped cause their own harm, but did not accept a known risk.

b.q: Tariq is hit by a cricket ball while sitting in a marked area of a ground, under a sign warning of flying balls. He sues the club. Which defence is the club most likely to use?
opts: Voluntary assumption of risk, which could defeat the claim
Voluntary assumption of risk, which would only cut damages
Contributory negligence, which could defeat the claim
Contributory negligence, which would only cut damages
b.why: Tariq knew the specific risk from the sign and chose to sit there, so voluntary assumption of risk fits. If proven, it can defeat the claim. Contributory negligence is tempting, but it is about failing to take care and only reduces damages.
b.clue: Tariq was warned of the risk and chose to stay. Think about what that defence can do to the claim.

a.best: The damages are reduced to reflect the passenger's share

b.best: Voluntary assumption of risk, which could defeat the claim

problems.detail: Two options and the why say contributory negligence 'only' cuts or reduces damages, where the card says the court 'can reduce' them. In Victoria, s 63 of the Wrongs Act 1958 lets a court reduce damages by up to 100% for contributory negligence, so 'only' overstates the limit.

The stem asks about 'this defence' without naming any defence. It reads as if a defence was already mentioned. It also tells the student that some defence applies, which rules out the 'damages are increased' option.

a.q: A court finds a driver negligent, but the injured passenger was not wearing a seatbelt, which made their injuries worse. If the driver raises this, what is the likely effect?
opts: The damages are reduced to reflect the passenger's share
The claim fails completely because the risk was accepted
The driver is found to owe no duty of care to the passenger
The driver is found not to have breached the duty of care
a.why: Not wearing a seatbelt is a failure to take reasonable care for one's own safety, so it is contributory negligence, which lets the court reduce the damages. a.clue: Did the passenger accept a known risk, or fail to take care?

b.q: Tariq is hit by a cricket ball while sitting in a marked area of a ground, under a sign warning of flying balls. He sues the club. Which defence is the club most likely to use?
opts: Voluntary assumption of risk, as he accepted a known risk
Contributory negligence, as he accepted a known risk
Voluntary assumption of risk, as the club breached its duty
Contributory negligence, as the club breached its duty
b.why: Tariq knew the specific risk from the sign and chose to sit there, so voluntary assumption of risk fits, and if proven it can defeat the claim. Contributory negligence is tempting, but it is about the plaintiff failing to take reasonable care, not knowingly accepting a risk. A breach by the club is part of proving negligence, not a defence.
b.clue: Tariq was warned of a specific risk and chose to stay.
